Six Ways to Score a Match

cv.matchTemplate takes a method argument with six values. Run all six on the game screenshot and on the face photo, and see which ones find the target, which one wants the minimum, and which one is fooled by bright pixels.

Minimum or maximum
The two TM_SQDIFF methods measure difference, so the best match is the smallest value: take min_loc from cv.minMaxLoc. Taking max_loc with them finds the worst match in the image. The other four measure similarity, and the best match is the largest.

    
Bright pixels fool the raw scores
TM_CCORR just adds up products, so a bright region scores high whatever its pattern. On the face photo its best match is the bottom-right corner, and on the game it lands on no icon at all. TM_CCOEFF subtracts the means but does not divide: on the game it lands on an icon, but not on the exact copy, and its values run into the millions, so no fixed threshold means anything.

    
The normalized ones
Only the three _NORMED methods give scores that mean the same thing everywhere, which is what a single threshold needs. TM_CCOEFF_NORMED is the normalized correlation of this lecture. Every value here is OpenCV's, on the color screenshot and the grayscale photo; the maps are shown at half size for the screenshot.
